messages.subject: Re: Next (baby) steps: Common blog?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'd like to step in the discussion and take the opportunity for a short introduction:

My name ist Felix Schönbrodt, I'm a PhD student working at the Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich (Germany).
I'm very happy that my GSoC proposal got accepted - I'm working with my mentor Stefan Schmukle on social relations analyses (a topic mainly relevant for psychologists and social sciences). Thanks to Dirk and all mentors for the effort put into the organization of the GSoC projects.

Concerning the "information flow", some thoughts of mine:

I see 4 possible target audiences for the information flow:

Internal communication:
1. Between students and mentors: I think, information between student and mentor should be set up according to their individual preferences
2. Between all current GSoC students: Students could inform each other about the current status of their own project and give mutual motivation

External communication:
3. Towards Google: "See how productive we are, and how successful we mentor and accomplish our projects. Next year, you can give us more of them ;-)"
4. Towards the R community: "Look, we have some very active and talented students, wisely guided by generous mentors. We are a great community. Check out the new projects!"

Personally, I am going to use R-Forge and the built-in mailing list for the internal communication of my project.

For points 2 - 4, I think a blog which documents the milestones of the 2010 projects (Which projects got accepted? Which were the major steps and obstacles? And a documentation and celebration of the results at the end of the period) would be a nice thing. Maybe it would be nice if it's integrated in the rest of the R infrastructure (e.g. in the R-Wiki), instead of setting up an "unconnected" external blog?

Concerning 4), an article in the R Journal would be nice.

Best,
Felix

messages.subject: Re: Next (baby) steps: Common blog?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

Following Felix's lead, I'll first introduce myself.

I'm Chidambaram (chillu) and I'm a student of Electrical Engineering at IIT, Kharagpur (India) working towards a Bachelors in Electrical and Masters in Control Sytems Engineering. I'm working with Prof. John Nash on building an Automatic Differentiation Engine in R.

And really a big thanks to Dirk for his dedication and patience (especially with me!).

I agree with Felix, in that the communication between the mentor and student is the most important and it should be in a form that both are comfortable with. In our case we have opted to use a wiki.

OTOH, it is also important to keep the community informed about important milestones so that people can know when the project has reached important milestones and is ready to be tinkered with. For this purpose I think its best to have a common blog where all the 2010 GSOC students from R can post so that the people from the R community can visit *one* place for all the updates relating to the GSOC projects. Possibly they can subscribe to the RSS feeds and keep themselves updated on the latest from the projects. (One could also argue that the R mailing lists are already the one place that R devs visit regularly and GSoC milestone announcements could be made here itself)

I think its important that we sort this out before the 20th of May, so that actual communication can take place subsequently in a form that everyone agrees on.

Regards,
Chillu

messages.subject: Next steps
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

A couple of days ago, I asked how you all felt about a little structure for
the overall progress messages.

 * Roger suggested r-forge, which was seconded by Felix who already set-up a
   repo and project there.  R-Forge is definitely a good option, its recent
   struggles with uptime and power over in Vienna notwithstanding.

 * Tal gave some tips for blogging and email-to-blig interfaces.  Shane
   seconded the choice of blogs.

 * Felix then gave a nice little breakdown of possible communication lines,
   from 'narrow' mentor-to-student to 'wider' community-oriented ones.

With that, led me explain better what I had in mind:

 - there is definitely need for student-mentor communication, and this
   mostly works in a natural way

 - the R Project has been successful (or just lucky :-) in the past without
   'enforcing' anything more; other project have reported success with some
   'wider' communications tools -- and blogs are one easy example

 - my role as admin in part encompasses playing 'backup' here, so I (as well
   as the R community as a whole) want to ensure that all the pieces remain
   in flow and moving.

Therefore, I would like to repeat to a suggestion to set 'something' up.
This could be a joint blogger.com <http://blogger.com> or wordpress account, or even just a wiki
page (preferably with a rss/atom feed though).

These two to three months tend to fly by quickly. Many past participants have
found it helpful to keep some sort of informal timeline -- maybe weekly or
bi-monthly -- to post some status updates.  More frequently works too.

So would anyone like to volunteer setting up a 'GSoC R 2010' blog account?
Or do to many of you are indifferent ?  I'd love to hear from our students
here, so (in alphabetical order) Chidambaram, Colin, Felix, Ian, Yasuhisa:
how do feel about this?

That concludes the nagging message of the week :)

--
  Regards, Dirk

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
For those who wants to start using the blog
http://gsoc2010r.wordpress.com/
There are two options:

Option 1: publish to blog via e-mail
You e-mail me (tal.g...@gmail.com) that you want to blog.  I reply to your e-mail, with sending you a "secret" e-mail.  Then, every time you wish to publish a new post, you simply send an e-mail to that address, and it will get publish.
Pros: simply e-mailing.  No need to learn anything.
Cons: You won't be able to fix things without asking someone with blog access to help.

Option 2: get direct blog access
You create a wordpress account (username, password, e-mail) via here:
http://en.wordpress.com/signup/
You e-mail me (tal.g...@gmail.com) you want to join the blog.  I add you to the blog, which will allow you to publish and edit your own posts (but not others).
Pros: You will be able to fix things in the posts by yourself
Cons: Will require you to take more steps.  This is probably the best for people with blogging experience (or people who wishes to learn about it through this experience)

I understand Felix agreed to work on the admin side also, so I believe that response time for questions could be good.

Best,
Tal

messages.body_plain:
For information of others.

This was one of my first concerns.

Chillu (student) and I (mentor) are using a wiki page with a "diary" subpage on my virtual
server at uOttawa. We haven't yet worked out how much global access to provide to this,
but in our Automatic Differentiation project there are several folk who've offered help.
Over next week or so we'll work out the access rules, likely something with global read,
limited write access. This is nominally easy with Dokuwiki, but I've been caught once or
twice in the past.

The diary page was helpful to me in a previous (unrelated) project. A bit messy but effective.

We haven't formalized what we'll do with code, but have been talking about svn on r-forge.

JN

That's very true. The diary will be terse and difficult to follow as far as journals go. The blog can inform a wider audience in a more coherent manner. I already have a couple of ideas in mind for a blog post on AD methods that I'm planning to blog on.

I will continue to maintain a diary (mostly for myself if not anyone else) and try to put in as many informative blog posts as I can to inform people too.

Group blogs serving a common interest are often remarkably successful. Few math blog examples that come to mind are the n-Category Cafe and the Secret Blogging Seminar among several others.

Hi everyone,

I'm just writing to update everyone about the web-based graphing proposal for Summer of Code. As you know, I didn't end up submitting a proposal, but this has been on my mind and I decided to build a simple prototype.
